section.title: New Heavens and a New Earth
section.sectionRationale: God answers the prayer of chapters 63-64 with a sweeping response: He was found by those who did not seek Him, He will judge the persistently rebellious, and He will create new heavens and a new earth so wonderful that the former things will not even be remembered. It is the fullest Old Testament picture of final, cosmic renewal before the book's closing chapter.
section.thesis: God reveals Himself to those who never sought Him while judging those who persistently provoke Him, and promises to create new heavens and a new earth where weeping is forgotten, life is no longer cut short, and even the ancient enmity of the serpent remains but harms no one on His holy mountain.
section.frameNote: Three movements: I revealed Myself to those who did not seek Me, an obstinate people confronted; My servants will eat while you go hungry, a stark reversal; and I create new heavens and a new earth, no more weeping, the wolf and the lamb together.

units.label: I revealed Myself to those who did not seek Me
units.note: an obstinate people who provoke Me

verses.text: “I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me; I was found by those who did not seek Me. To a nation that did not call My name, I said, ‘Here I am! Here I am!’
All day long I have held out My hands to an obstinate people who walk in the wrong path, who follow their own imaginations,
to a people who continually provoke Me to My face, sacrificing in the gardens and burning incense on altars of brick,
sitting among the graves, spending nights in secret places, eating the meat of pigs and polluted broth from their bowls.
They say, ‘Keep to yourself; do not come near me, for I am holier than you!’ Such people are smoke in My nostrils, a fire that burns all day long.
Behold, it is written before Me: I will not keep silent, but I will repay; I will pay it back into their laps,

both for your iniquities and for those of your fathers,” says the LORD. “Because they burned incense on the mountains and scorned Me on the hills, I will measure into their laps full payment for their former deeds.”

units.label: My servants will eat, you will go hungry
units.note: a blessing preserved, a judgment coming

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “As the new wine is found in a cluster of grapes, and men say, ‘Do not destroy it, for it contains a blessing,’ so I will act on behalf of My servants; I will not destroy them all.
And I will bring forth descendants from Jacob, and heirs from Judah; My elect will possess My mountains, and My servants will dwell there.
Sharon will become a pasture for flocks, and the Valley of Achor a resting place for herds, for My people who seek Me.
But you who forsake the LORD, who forget My holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and fill bowls of mixed wine for Destiny,

I will destine you for the sword, and you will all kneel down to be slaughtered, because I called and you did not answer, I spoke and you did not listen; you did evil in My sight and chose that in which I did not delight.”
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: “My servants will eat, but you will go hungry; My servants will drink, but you will go thirsty; My servants will rejoice, but you will be put to shame.
My servants will shout for joy with a glad heart, but you will cry out with a heavy heart and wail with a broken spirit.
You will leave behind your name as a curse for My chosen ones, and the Lord GOD will slay you; but to His servants He will give another name.

Whoever invokes a blessing in the land will do so by the God of truth, and whoever takes an oath in the land will swear by the God of truth. For the former troubles will be forgotten and hidden from My sight.

units.label: New heavens and a new earth
units.note: no more weeping, the wolf and lamb together

verses.text: For behold, I will {{baraOlam|create new heavens and a new earth}}. The former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.
But be glad and rejoice forever in what I create; for I will create Jerusalem to be a joy and its people to be a delight.
I will rejoice in Jerusalem and take delight in My people. The sounds of weeping and crying will no longer be heard in her.

No longer will a nursing infant live but a few days, or an old man fail to live out his years. For the youth will die at a hundred years, and he who fails to reach a hundred will be considered accursed.
They will build houses and dwell in them; they will plant vineyards and eat their fruit.

No longer will they build houses for others to inhabit, nor plant for others to eat. For as is the lifetime of a tree, so will be the days of My people, and My chosen ones will fully enjoy the work of their hands.
They will not labor in vain or bear children doomed to disaster; for they will be a people blessed by the LORD, they and their descendants with them.
Even before they call, I will answer, and while they are still speaking, I will hear.

The wolf and the lamb will feed together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox, but the food of the serpent will be dust. They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain,” says the LORD.

baraOlam.gloss: To create new heavens and a new earth, using bara, the same verb reserved in Hebrew exclusively for God's own creative act, as in Genesis 1:1. This is not mere repair but a fresh act of divine creation, the ground for Peter's and John's New Testament promise of new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells, 2 Peter 3:13, Revelation 21:1.

basic.context: God answers the desperate lament of chapters 63-64 with a sweeping oracle: He reveals Himself even to those who never sought Him, judges those who persistently provoke Him with idolatry, and finally promises to create entirely new heavens and a new earth, so wonderful that the old troubles will not even come to mind.
basic.hermeneutics: This oracle deliberately holds together sharp, real judgment on the unrepentant and lavish, unearned promise for God's servants; the new heavens and new earth are not a vague spiritual metaphor but a real, physical renewal, described with concrete pictures, long life, secure homes, resolved conflict between predator and prey.
basic.originalLanguages: God's promise to bara, create, new heavens and a new earth uses the exact Hebrew verb reserved for God's original creative act in Genesis 1:1, marking this as a genuinely new act of creation, not mere repair, the foundation for the New Testament's own promise of new heavens and a new earth.
basic.typology: Paul quotes verse 1 directly of Gentiles finding God though they did not seek Him, Romans 10:20. The new heavens and new earth of verse 17 become the direct template for 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1. The wolf and lamb feeding together echoes and extends Isaiah 11:6-9's picture of messianic peace.
basic.christ: Paul applies verse 1 explicitly to God's revealing Himself to Gentiles who did not seek Him, Romans 10:20, part of his argument for the gospel's reach beyond Israel through Christ. And the new heavens and new earth promised here are directly named again, almost verbatim, in 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1, both understood as fulfilled through Christ's death, resurrection, and final return.
basic.god: God is patient beyond expectation, holding out His hands all day long to an obstinate people, yet He is also just, refusing to let persistent, willful provocation go unanswered; His mercy to the undeserving and His justice toward the unrepentant are both fully real, held together without contradiction.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 10:20 quotes verse 1 of Gentiles finding God though they did not seek Him. 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1 both promise new heavens and a new earth, directly building on this chapter. Isaiah 11:6-9 shares the wolf-and-lamb imagery of restored creation.
basic.oneStory: God's revealing Himself to those who never sought Him, His justice toward the unrepentant, and His promise of an entirely new creation trace one continuous line from this chapter through Paul's gospel to Peter's and John's visions of the world made new, all converging on the same certainty, God is making all things new, and He has already begun in Christ.

context.literary:
Chapter 65 is built as an answer, and the answer is addressed to the prayer that precedes it. The lament of 64:12 ended with two questions, 'will You restrain Yourself? Will You keep silent?' God opens by saying that He has not been silent or hidden, and that the problem lay on the other side. 'I revealed Myself... I was found... I said, Here I am! Here I am!' The same chapter closes on 65:24, 'Even before they call, I will answer,' so the whole reply is wrapped in a promise of answered prayer. The first half has Him calling to people who 'did not call My name,' and the last has Him answering people who have not yet called.

The chapter then moves in three blocks. Verses 1 to 7 describe the people who provoke Him, a charge sheet of cult practices closing with a 'written' record that He will repay. Verses 8 to 16 split the community into two groups. 'My servants' and 'you' are set side by side in a run of matched reversals: eat and go hungry, drink and go thirsty, rejoice and be put to shame, shout for joy and cry out with a heavy heart, a new name for one group and a name left behind as a curse for the other. Verses 17 to 25 then widen the lens from a divided community to a remade cosmos.

The last section is organised around the verb 'create.' It appears at the head of verse 17 and twice in verse 18, and what is created is both the heavens and earth and 'Jerusalem to be a joy.' After that the poem goes down a list of ordinary sorrows and deletes each one: weeping, early death, building for others, working in vain, children doomed to disaster. The final verse brings in the animals of Isaiah 11 and closes on the serpent's food of dust, so that the picture of the redeemed world ends on a quiet reminder of the first curse.
context.historical:
The charge sheet in verses 3 to 5 describes the religion of a community that is formally Israelite and practically syncretist. Sacrificing 'in the gardens' recalls the sacred groves that Isaiah 1:29 had already condemned, and Isaiah 57:3 to 10 gives a longer picture of the same behaviour under the oaks and in the valleys. 'Sitting among the graves' and 'spending nights in secret places' suggest consulting the dead, which Isaiah 8:19 had warned against. Eating the meat of pigs touched the clear boundary of Leviticus 11:7. In verse 11 the people set a table for Fortune and fill the wine bowls for Destiny, and the BSB footnote names Gad and Meni as gods of fortune and fate. These were gods of luck in a world where an exile and return had made people feel their fate was uncertain.

The prophet's audience is divided. The 'holier than thou' voice of verse 5 comes from people who are treating their own ritual distinctiveness as a protection from the LORD. The faithful are named as 'My servants' and 'My elect,' and the line between them runs through the community and not around it. That fits the picture of the early second temple period in Haggai, Zechariah 8 and Nehemiah 13, where the returnees were a mixed body with real disagreements about worship and purity.

The geography of verse 10 is chosen. Sharon was the fertile coastal plain on the west, and the Valley of Achor lay on the east towards Jericho. It was named for the trouble that Achan brought on Israel, Joshua 7:24 to 26, and Hosea 2:15 had already promised to turn it into 'a gateway of hope.' The promise of building houses and eating the fruit of the vineyards, verses 21 and 22, undoes the curses of Deuteronomy 28:30 to 33, where the covenant breaker builds and does not live in the house, plants and does not enjoy the fruit. The first hearers would have heard the promise as the covenant curses reversed.
context.canonical:
The chapter is one of the most used in the New Testament's account of the future. Paul quotes the opening verses in Romans 10:20 and 21, using the first for the Gentiles who found God without seeking and the second for Israel's long refusal. Peter's 'we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells,' 2 Peter 3:13, restates Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22, and John's 'Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth' opens the last vision of the Bible, Revelation 21:1. Several details of Revelation 21:1 to 4 echo this chapter: the former things passing away, the city as a joy and a bride, and the end of weeping.

The movement from exclusion to inclusion connects with the earlier chapters of Isaiah. Isaiah 56:3 to 8 had already welcomed foreigners and eunuchs, and Hosea 2:23, 'I will say to those called Not My People, You are My people,' is the same pattern which Peter applies to the church in 1 Peter 2:10. Isaiah 25:6 to 8 promised a feast and the swallowing of death, and Isaiah 51:3 promised a wilderness made like Eden. The wolf and the lamb of verse 25 return Isaiah 11:6 to 9, and the serpent's dust takes up Genesis 3:14.

Jesus' beatitudes and woes in Luke 6:21 and 25 follow the same pattern as the servant and rebel contrast of verses 13 and 14: those who hunger and weep now will be filled and will laugh, and those who are full and laughing will go hungry and weep.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet wanted two groups in the community to hear two different things from one speech. To the faithful who had just prayed in anguish, he wanted to say that their prayer was heard before it was prayed, and that the God they were asking to come down had been standing with open hands all along. To the compromised insiders, he wanted to say that proximity to the temple or to the covenant name is no shelter. A person can be a descendant of Jacob and sit among the graves and eat what the law forbids, and the LORD counts that as provocation to His face.

He also meant to redefine who 'My servants' are. The category is not ethnic and not institutional. It consists of those who seek Him, who answer when He calls and who tremble at His word, and the 'nation that did not call My name' is invited in on the same terms. The sorting out is the LORD's work and is not left to human zeal.

Finally he gave the listeners a hope large enough to outlast the disappointments of the return. Those who had come back expecting glory and found hardship were told that God was about to do something that would make even the memory of the grief unnecessary. The hope is concrete, houses, vineyards, children and old age, because it is meant to be believed by people who live in a damaged world and need to know that their daily labour is not futile.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records two things at once, what God says He will do and what He saw His people doing. The charge list of verses 3 to 5, with its gardens, graves and pork, is a description of sin and not a manual of what believers should avoid in exactly those forms. What carries over is the principle underneath it: religion that carries on with God's name while trusting luck and fate is rebellion, and a claim of holiness that pushes others away, 'Keep to yourself,' is the very thing that burns in God's nostrils.

The promises of the final section are descriptive of the world to come and not a guarantee of individual outcomes in the present. Verses 20 to 23 do not tell a believer that a child will not die or that every harvest will be eaten by the one who planted. Scripture itself, Romans 8:22 and 23, says believers groan with the creation. What the promises do is give the shape of the hope, and they are meant to make Christians the kind of people who work for the signs of it now, by caring for infants, the old, homes and fair labour, without claiming that the present age has delivered the whole.

The opening verses model another thing: a prayer that God answers by taking the initiative. Believers are not told that their seeking earns the finding. They are told that God was the first to say, 'Here I am,' Romans 10:20.

debates.question: Is the 'new heavens and a new earth' a replacement of the present creation or its renewal?

views.label: Replacement, the old order is destroyed and a new one made
views.case: Isaiah says 'create,' 'The former things will not be remembered,' and 2 Peter 3:10 speaks of the heavens disappearing with a roar and the elements being destroyed by fire. Revelation 21:1 says 'the first heaven and earth had passed away.' On this reading the language describes a real discontinuity, with new material made after the old is gone.

views.label: Renewal, the same creation purified and remade
views.case: Paul says the creation itself 'will be set free from its bondage to decay,' Romans 8:21, and Jesus speaks of 'the renewal of all things,' Matthew 19:28. Peter's fire is a fire of refining and exposure, so that the earth 'will be laid bare,' 2 Peter 3:10, and Isaiah's new creation is full of recognisable houses, vineyards and a Jerusalem. The risen body, which is the same body made new, is the pattern.

views.label: Poetic language for a renewed community in history
views.case: Some read verses 18 to 25 as pictures of a restored Jerusalem within history, in the way Isaiah 51:16 speaks of the prophet's words establishing the heavens and founding the earth. They point to the presence of death and sin in verse 20 as a sign that the text describes a better age in this world.

debates.bearing: The New Testament authors read Isaiah 65 as pointing to the final new creation, and whichever way the question of continuity is settled, the text insists that the new world is physical, righteous and God's own act. The third view takes seriously verse 20's mention of death, which the next debate considers.

debates.question: How can there still be death and a sinner in verse 20 if the world is made new?

views.label: The vision is of an age before the final state
views.case: Revelation 20 describes a thousand year reign before the last judgment, and many who read it literally place verse 20 in that period, where death is greatly reduced but not yet abolished. Revelation 21:4, with 'no more death,' then belongs to the later stage.

views.label: Poetic use of Old Testament categories
views.case: In a culture where early death was the commonest sorrow, to live a full span was the picture of blessing. Verse 20 is using that currency of the day, a hundred years being a very full life, and the point is the end of premature loss. It is a way of saying 'no more untimely grief' and not a timetable.

views.label: Progressive revelation, a picture later made clearer
views.case: Isaiah 25:8 had said God 'will swallow up death forever.' The prophet may hold a picture of a world very much better than this one in the same breath as the promise that death is finished, and the New Testament sharpens what Isaiah says in pieces.

debates.bearing: Each reading takes the text seriously and each admits that verse 20 is less than the whole promise. A reader can safely hold the central claim, that God will end the sorrows listed, without settling the sequence.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening verses are carried by two verbs in a stem that is reflexive or passive in form. 'I revealed Myself' and 'I was found' both come from the Niphal, a stem that can mean 'allowed Myself to be asked' and 'allowed Myself to be found.' The nuance is that God put Himself within reach. The people did not ask and did not seek, and He still let Himself be found. Paul quotes the Greek form in Romans 10:20 to say that the finding was an act of grace. The doubled 'Here I am! Here I am!' uses the word hineni, the very word Isaiah gave to God when he said 'Here am I. Send me!' in Isaiah 6:8, and the word God promises to say to those who cry out in Isaiah 58:9. The God who was asked to come down answers with the prophet's own word.

In verse 2 the 'obstinate' people are described by a word, sorer, which means stubborn and refractory. It is the word Deuteronomy 21:18 uses for 'a stubborn and rebellious son.' The 'hands held out' translate a phrase for spreading out the palms, the gesture of the pleading or the welcoming, so the picture is of a parent with open arms facing a child who turns his back.

The pun in verses 11 and 12 is hidden in English. Meni, the god of fate, comes from the root for counting out or assigning, and verse 12 says 'I will destine you for the sword,' where the verb is of the same root as the name. The people have laid a table for a deity of allotment and God allots them to the sword. The BSB footnote names Gad as a god of fortune and Meni as a god of fate.

Verses 17 and 18 use the verb bara, the word for the creative acts of God from Genesis 1:1, three times in two verses, and in participle form, 'I am creating,' so the action is already under way. Verse 18 says God will create Jerusalem as 'rejoicing' and its people as 'joy,' two nouns in a line of Hebrew parallelism, and the city is thereby defined by its effect. The phrase 'come to mind' is literally 'go up on the heart,' a Hebrew idiom for remembrance, so the old sorrows will not rise up in anyone's thoughts. 'Former things' echoes Isaiah 43:18 and 19, where God said, 'Do not call to mind the former things... Behold, I am about to do something new.'

The 'God of truth' in verse 16 is, literally, the God of the Amen. The footnote does not mention it, but the root is the one behind 'faithful' and 'truth,' and the New Testament picks it up when Jesus is called 'the Amen,' Revelation 3:14, and when Paul says that all the promises of God are 'Yes' in Christ and that through Him 'our Amen is spoken,' 2 Corinthians 1:20.

Verse 22 says 'My chosen ones will fully enjoy the work of their hands.' The verb is one that literally means to wear out, so the idea is that they will use their handiwork until it is worn through, instead of having it taken from them. The final clause of verse 25, 'the food of the serpent will be dust,' echoes Genesis 3:14, 'dust you will eat,' and the BSB footnote notes that the word is the same word, nachash.

typology.fulfillment: The prophet is speaking first of Israelites who had drifted from God, and he describes God as stepping toward people who were not looking. Paul reads the line as covering the Gentiles who found God without having sought Him, Romans 10:20, and joins it to Hosea 2:23, where those called 'Not My People' become God's people, which Peter applies to the church, 1 Peter 2:10. The correspondence is that grace moves first toward people with no claim. The escalation is that in Christ the offer goes to every nation. The type falls short because the passage also speaks of those who persist in refusal, and Paul uses verse 2 of Israel's disobedience, so the pattern is both promise and warning.

Achor was the valley of trouble, where Achan's sin was judged, Joshua 7:24 to 26. Hosea 2:15 turned it into a gateway of hope, and Isaiah 65:10 makes it a resting place for herds. The correspondence is that a place named for judgment becomes a place of rest. In Christ, the cross is the place of judgment where trouble was borne, and the result is rest for His people, Matthew 11:28. The text does not make Achor a symbol of the cross, so this is a pattern and not a prediction. The type falls short because Achor is a real valley and the promise concerns the land, while the gospel reaches to every place.

typology.type: The new heavens and new earth, Isaiah 65:17
typology.fulfillment: The promise of a created new order begins to come true in Christ. Paul says, 'if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!' 2 Corinthians 5:17, and in Galatians 6:15 says that 'what counts is a new creation.' Christ is 'the firstfruits' of the resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:20, so the new creation has already started in one body. The escalation is from a promise about the cosmos to a person who is its beginning, and from the future to a present foretaste. The type is not yet complete, because Revelation 21:1 still looks for the world itself to be made new.

typology.type: The wolf, the lamb and the serpent's dust, Isaiah 65:25
typology.fulfillment: The curse in Genesis 3:14 sentenced the serpent to eat dust, and Isaiah's last clause sets the old enemy in the new creation harmless and humbled, while the predators and prey lie down together. In Christ the head of the serpent is crushed, Hebrews 2:14, and Paul promises that 'the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet,' Romans 16:20. The escalation is from a picture of the curse's end to a decisive victory won by a person. The type falls short because Isaiah's serpent remains, though without harm, whereas Revelation says that the devil is thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10.

study.christ:
The first link is Paul's use of the opening verse. In Romans 10:20 he says, 'And Isaiah boldly says: I was found by those who did not seek Me; I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me,' and he hears it as the story of the gospel's reach to the nations. The speaker of that verse is the LORD, and the Gospels show Jesus doing what the verse describes. He says that He came 'to seek and to save the lost,' Luke 19:10. He stands at the door and knocks, Revelation 3:20, and He tells of a father who ran to meet a son while he was still far off, Luke 15:20, which is the human picture of 'before they call, I will answer.' The 'Here I am' of God becomes in Christ a visible presence among people who had not asked for Him, John 1:14.

The second link is the new creation. Isaiah 65:17 is the root promise, and the New Testament insists that the new creation begins with Christ. He is 'the firstfruits' of those who have died, 1 Corinthians 15:20, 'the beginning and firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:18, and the one through whom God will 'reconcile to Himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through the blood of His cross,' Colossians 1:20. When John sees the new heaven and the new earth, the voice from the throne says, 'Behold, I make all things new,' Revelation 21:5, and the 'Behold' answers the 'behold' of Isaiah 65:17. That the One on the throne is also the Lamb, Revelation 22:3, shows who is doing the creating.

The third link is the joy. God says, 'I will rejoice in Jerusalem and take delight in My people.' It is Zephaniah 3:17 in different words, and Hebrews says that Jesus endured the cross 'for the joy set before Him,' Hebrews 12:2. The city that is created to be a joy becomes the bride 'prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2. Christ's own delight is bound up with the people He redeems.

The fourth link is the division of the community. The contrast between the servants who eat and the rebels who go hungry is repeated in Jesus' own words, 'Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled... Woe to you who are well fed now, for you will hunger,' Luke 6:21 and 25. And the new name of verse 15 returns in the promise to the overcomer of 'a white stone inscribed with a new name,' Revelation 2:17.

A caution is in order. Isaiah 65 does not name the Messiah, and not every detail, such as the Valley of Achor or the precise hundred years of verse 20, is a coded reference to Jesus. The links above rest on the way the New Testament itself picks up the chapter and on the bridges of the book of Isaiah as a whole. What the chapter offers is the destination of Christ's work: a creation set right, a people gathered from every nation, and a God who answers before He is asked.
study.god:
The chapter begins by showing a God who takes the first step. He says He was ready to be asked and ready to be found by those who did neither. That is grace in its plainest form, and it explains the shape of the Bible's story: God comes looking. The 'Here I am! Here I am!' is the sound of urgency, and the long phrase 'all day long I have held out My hands' is a picture of patience that does not tire. Paul quotes it in Romans 10:21 to say that Israel's rejection was met by a God who kept the invitation open, and Peter says that He is patient, 'not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance,' 2 Peter 3:9.

The same chapter is as plain about His justice. The God who holds out His hands is the God who says 'it is written before Me,' verse 6, that He keeps a record and will repay. He does not forget what His people did and what their fathers did. He is not provoked into sudden rage but is provoked 'to My face' by what is done in His sight, and it is that persistent offence that He answers. Revelation 20:12 repeats the picture of the books. The text does not set mercy and judgment in competition. Both are the way a holy God deals with people He has loved.

The chapter shows God as one who preserves. 'As the new wine is found in a cluster of grapes, and men say, Do not destroy it, for it contains a blessing, so I will act on behalf of My servants,' verse 8. A bunch of grapes with some good juice is saved for what is in it, and God treats His people the same way. For the sake of the blessing He will not destroy them all. It gives a doctrine of the remnant that rests on His faithfulness and not on the number of the faithful.

He is the creator who can begin again. The verb is bara, the verb of Genesis 1, in the present participle, so that it is not a repair but a new act of the one who made everything. That makes the final hope depend on His power. He also takes delight: 'I will rejoice in Jerusalem and take delight in My people.' The Lord of heaven has joy in His creatures, and the end of the story is shaped by His gladness.

He is the God who attends to the ordinary. The new creation is not a haze of glory but a place where infants live, old men reach their years, houses are built and lived in, and vineyards are eaten by the people who planted them. It also shows His concern with the injuries of the curse in Genesis 3, toil and death and pain. He answers before they call, which shows both His knowledge and His nearness, and He is called 'the God of truth,' the God of the Amen, who keeps His word.

For worship, the chapter calls for gratitude that He seeks, for humility, since the people who 'say, Keep to yourself, for I am holier than you' are in danger, and for hope that is as concrete as His promises. We can pray expecting to be heard, because He has already said He listens.

crossReferences.note: Paul quotes verse 1 for the Gentiles who found God without seeking Him and verse 2 for Israel's disobedience, so the two halves of the opening of Isaiah 65 describe the gospel's two outcomes. He calls Isaiah 'bold' for saying it.

God promises to say to those called 'Not My People' that they are His people. The pattern of grace reaching the outsider is the same as in Isaiah 65:1, and Peter later applies this line to the church in 1 Peter 2:10.

'Do not call to mind the former things... Behold, I am about to do something new.' The same pair of former and new things recurs in 65:17, which turns the earlier promise of a new exodus into the promise of a new creation.

A longer picture of the idolatry named in 65:3 to 7, with oaks, valleys, sacrifices to the dead and service of other gods. Reading it beside chapter 65 shows that the charge is not a passing comment but a persistent pattern in the book's last section.

Among the covenant curses is building a house and not living in it, planting a vineyard and not enjoying its fruit. Isaiah 65:21 and 22 reverses these curses line for line, so the new creation is also the end of the covenant curse.

The Valley of Achor becomes 'a gateway of hope.' It is the nearest prophetic partner to Isaiah 65:10, where the same valley is a resting place for herds, and it shows a place of judgment turned to a place of mercy.

The wolf and the lamb, the lion and the ox, and the promise that nothing will harm or destroy on God's holy mountain. Isaiah 65:25 repeats the picture in short form and ties it to the knowledge of the LORD that fills the earth.

The serpent is sentenced to eat dust. The last clause of Isaiah 65:25 reaches back to it and sets the old enemy in the new world as a defeated and powerless creature, so that the story that began with the curse ends with its limit.

Peter describes the day of the Lord, with the heavens passing away and the elements melting, and then says 'we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells.' It is a direct appeal to Isaiah's promise and sets out how Christians should live while they wait.

John's last vision takes up Isaiah 65:17 to 19 almost phrase by phrase: a new heaven and earth, a Jerusalem prepared as a joy, no more weeping, and the former things gone. The voice from the throne says, 'Behold, I make all things new.'
Paul says anyone in Christ is a new creation. The promise of Isaiah 65 has already begun in believers, which is why Christians can be said to live partly in the new world while still in the old.

While Daniel was still praying, Gabriel came with the news that an answer had gone out at the start of his petitions. It is a narrative picture of Isaiah 65:24, 'while they are still speaking, I will hear,' and shows how an exile's prayer might be met.

Jesus' blessings and woes reverse the fortunes of the hungry and the full in the same way as Isaiah 65:13 and 14. Those who hunger and weep now will be filled and will laugh, and those who have everything now will hunger and mourn.

A feast on God's mountain for all peoples, the swallowing up of death forever and the wiping away of tears. It supplies the large context for the banquet and the end of weeping in Isaiah 65:13 and 19, and Revelation 21:4 draws on it as well.

study.oneStory:
Genesis opened with a creation God called good and a curse that fell on the serpent, the woman and the ground. Isaiah 65 reaches back across the whole story to that curse and takes it apart piece by piece. The pain of childbearing, the toil of working the ground and the return to dust that were spelled out in Genesis 3:16 to 19 reappear here as 'children doomed to disaster,' labour in vain and early death, and each is undone. The serpent's dust, from Genesis 3:14, is the only part of the old order that stays, and it stays as a sign of defeat.

The chapter also answers the question the exile had left open, which was whether God's promises to Abraham could survive Israel's failure. It does so in two moves. One is that God sets apart a remnant who will inherit the mountains, verse 9, the continuation of the people through whom the nations were to be blessed. The other is that He opens the door wider, to a nation that did not call His name, verse 1. That is the Abrahamic promise of blessing for all the families of the earth, Genesis 12:3, carried forward to the point where Paul can quote it as the gospel's own story.

Between Isaiah and the end, the pivot is Christ. He is the one who brings the unseeking into the household, Ephesians 2:19, whose resurrection is the start of the new creation, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and whose Spirit makes believers 'a new creation' even now, 2 Corinthians 5:17. In the present the people of God are living in the overlap, with new life working in a world still marked by the curse, Romans 8:22 and 23. They build, plant and raise children in hope and are careful not to claim for this age what belongs to the next.

The story ends where Isaiah said it would. 'I will create new heavens and a new earth' becomes 'Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth,' Revelation 21:1. The God who said 'Here I am' is the God who dwells with man, Revelation 21:3. The city that Isaiah called a joy is the city whose gates never close, Revelation 21:25, and the tree of life that the garden lost grows again by the river, Revelation 22:2. The final answer to the lament of Isaiah 64 is a world in which no one has to ask where God is.

quiz.q: How does Paul use Isaiah 65:1 in Romans 10:20?

options.text: He applies it to Gentiles finding God through the gospel though they did not seek Him.
options.note: Romans 10:20 quotes this verse directly of Gentile inclusion in salvation.

options.text: He applies it only to ethnic Israel's continued search for God.
options.note: This reverses Paul's actual point; he applies the verse specifically to Gentiles, in contrast to Israel's response described in surrounding verses.

options.text: He uses it to prove that no one can ever find God.
options.note: The verse is used to show God can be found by those who did not seek Him, not that no one can find Him.

quiz.q: What is significant about the Hebrew verb translated 'create' in verse 17?

options.text: It is bara, the same verb used exclusively of God's original creative act in Genesis 1:1, signaling genuine new creation, not mere repair.
options.note: Bara marks this as an act of fresh divine creation.

options.text: It is a common word for building or renovating, used interchangeably for any construction.
options.note: Bara is reserved specifically for divine creative acts in the Hebrew Bible.

options.text: It refers only to planting a garden, unrelated to cosmic creation.
options.note: Garden imagery does appear elsewhere in this book, but this verb applies to the entire new heavens and new earth, not merely horticulture.

options.text: It is used here for the first time in the Hebrew Bible.
options.note: The verb bara appears earlier, notably in Genesis 1:1, which is precisely why its reuse here is significant.

quiz.q: How does verse 25's picture of the wolf and lamb relate to the rest of Isaiah?

options.text: It echoes and extends the same peaceable-kingdom imagery from Isaiah 11:6-9 of restored creation under the Messiah's reign.
options.note: Both passages share nearly identical imagery of former predators and prey living in peace.

options.text: It contradicts Isaiah 11's imagery and should be read as unrelated.
options.note: The imagery closely parallels and extends Isaiah 11, not contradicts it.

options.text: It refers only to literal agricultural practices with no symbolic meaning.
options.note: Real animals are pictured, but the imagery is widely understood as symbolic of cosmic peace and restored creation, not merely literal husbandry.

options.text: It is the only place in Isaiah where this imagery appears.
options.note: Isaiah 11:6-9 contains very similar imagery earlier in the book.

quiz.q: What two realities does this chapter hold together concerning God's people?

options.text: God's extraordinary patience toward the obstinate and His real justice against those who persistently refuse Him.
options.note: Verses 1-7 show patience and provocation together, and verses 11-15 show sharp, real judgment alongside blessing for God's servants.

options.text: That God shows patience but never actually judges anyone.
options.note: Verses 11-15 describe real, specific judgment on the unrepentant.

options.text: That God judges everyone equally with no distinction between servants and the obstinate.
options.note: God's justice is impartial in principle, but this chapter draws a sharp distinction in outcome between My servants and those who forsake the LORD.

options.text: That patience and justice are contradictory and cannot coexist in this passage.
options.note: The chapter presents both as fully real and consistent aspects of God's character.

questions: God says He revealed Himself to those who did not ask for Him. Where in your own life did God pursue you before you ever thought to seek Him?

The chapter names specific, real idolatry, sacrificing in gardens, seeking omens, worship of Fortune and Destiny. What modern equivalents of chasing luck or superstition compete for your trust in God's provision?
God promises a day when former troubles will be forgotten and hidden from His sight. What past grief or failure do you need to trust God can truly make new rather than define your future?

The new creation includes long life, secure homes, and labor that is not in vain. What area of your work or life currently feels like labor in vain that you can bring to God in hope of this promised renewal?
Even before they call, I will answer, verse 24. Is there a prayer you have stopped bringing to God because you assumed He was not listening?

translationNotes.note: Fortune and Destiny translate the names of two Babylonian or Canaanite deities, Gad and Meni, associated with luck and fate; the reference confirms specific, concrete idolatrous practice rather than a generic complaint.

The picture of very long life spans, a youth dying at a hundred years, uses hyperbolic covenant-blessing language common to describe an era of unprecedented flourishing, later read in its fullest sense as describing the eternal state.
